about: The names the network's lookups may be answered for once the DNS policy blocks the rest (S68 audit finding 14; dns-policy.bicep). Each entry is a name or a zone ending in a dot, and covers every name under it. Read from three days of staging's lookups (S78, 30 Sep to 3 Oct 2026), each one Microsoft's or GitHub's, and from the names those lookups pass through (S84, 3 to 5 Oct): the policy judges every name in a CNAME chain, so a name we allow whose chain runs through one we don't still reached the catch-all; names Microsoft picks and changes (storage accounts, the cluster's API host) are allowed by their zone, and so are zones where no customer can point a name at a server they run (Entra's, Key Vault's and Microsoft's edge networks); in zones any customer can create names in (Traffic Manager, Front Door's and Azure CDN's, Akamai's three), only the exact names the chains pass through, which Microsoft may change: the logs are read again before the catch-all blocks. An exact name covers names under it too, and Traffic Manager takes a dotted profile name (`x.mcr` was available, S84), but a profile only points at a fixed target, which the catch-all judges in turn: what is left is which of several such profiles is looked up, and a profile's query counts its owner sees, a narrow channel resting on the same CNAME question as below (Carry-Forward). Not listed on purpose: reverse lookups (Azure sends them to public servers, which answer that no such name exists), and the login service's internal address (answered inside the environment: it never appears in the logs). This narrows which names are answered; whether a blocked name's labels still reach its own server (Azure follows CNAME chains, so it may resolve a name before judging it) is proven before relying on it (Carry-Forward). The policy's dns-allow rule refuses any Allow not listed here.
